front: Why is glycogen more branched than amylopectin useful?
back: More chain ends, so glucose is released faster for the high energy demands of animals.

front: Why is an insoluble store useful?
back: It does not lower water potential (no osmotic water uptake) and cannot diffuse out of the cell.
β-glucose, β-1,4 glycosidic bonds; alternate units rotated 180°.

front: What gives cellulose its tensile strength?
back: Straight chains held by many hydrogen bonds into microfibrils, bundled into fibres in layers.
Amylopectin about every 24–30 units; glycogen about every 8–12 units.

front: Why can humans not digest cellulose?
back: No enzyme to hydrolyse β-1,4 glycosidic bonds.

front: Where are starch and glycogen stored?
back: Starch: grains in plant cells (seeds, tubers). Glycogen: granules in liver and muscle cells.
